items.definition: Seizing a device correctly so the evidence is preserved and usable in court.
items.examples: Photograph the screen, put the phone in a Faraday bag, record the chain of custody.
items.examTip: A Faraday bag blocks all signals, so the device can't be remotely wiped.
keyFacts: Collect passwords, chargers and cables, so the device can be accessed and kept powered
Keep its power state if possible, because turning it off loses data held in RAM
Isolate it with airplane mode or a Faraday bag, so it can't be remotely wiped or altered
Package it and record chain of custody, so the evidence is admissible in court

items.definition: Making an exact copy (image) of a system and analysing it with forensic tools.
items.examples: Imaging a drive, then reviewing logs and user activity.
items.examTip: Always analyse the COPY, never the original.
keyFacts: Take an exact (bit-for-bit) image, so analysis never touches the original evidence
Use forensic tools, which are tested and accepted in court
Review files, logs and user activity to build a timeline of what happened
Look for malware activity, to find out how the attacker got in and what they did

items.definition: The difficulties of collecting evidence from a system that is still running.
items.examples: Capturing RAM before it is lost at power-off.
items.examTip: RAM and temporary files are lost when the device is switched off.
keyFacts: Data keeps changing while the system runs, so evidence can be overwritten as you collect it
Risk of corrupting data, because the investigator's actions alter the live system
RAM and remote data are hard to capture, but may hold vital evidence such as encryption keys

items.definition: Collecting and analysing evidence from network devices after an incident.
items.examples: Reviewing firewall and router logs to trace an attacker.
items.examTip: Agree a method, get permission, and don't disrupt the live system.
keyFacts: Agree the methodology with the authorities, so the evidence is collected in an accepted way
Get permission first, because monitoring a network without authority can itself be illegal
Use passive and active tools: passive only watches traffic, active probes devices
Check firewall, switch, router and server logs, which record who connected and when

items.definition: Recording the incident scene thoroughly and at the time.
items.examples: Photos, diagrams, notes made on the spot, witness statements.
items.examTip: Contemporaneous notes = made at the time. They make evidence more reliable.
keyFacts: Secure the scene, so nobody can tamper with the evidence
Photos and diagrams record exactly how devices and cables were set up
Contemporaneous notes are written at the time, so they are accurate and trusted in court
Witness statements capture what people saw before memories fade

items.definition: Keeping exact copies of the system to compare against a clean original.
items.examples: Imaging a whole drive and hashing it to prove it hasn't changed.
items.examTip: Physical image = the whole drive, including deleted files. Targeted image = selected files only.
keyFacts: Keep a clean original for comparison, so changes made by an attacker can be spotted
Hash copies to prove they're unchanged, because matching hashes show nothing was altered
Capture disk, files and memory, so no evidence is missed
Include deleted and temporary files, which often hold evidence the attacker tried to hide

items.definition: Documenting every finding and action so the evidence is reliable.
items.examples: Logging every action, by whom, with timestamps.
items.examTip: Nothing should change the data; a competent person collects it; keep a chain of custody.
keyFacts: No action should change the data, so the evidence stays reliable
Collected by a competent person, so the methods can stand up in court
Chain of custody for every action, showing who had the evidence at all times
Record who made each decision, so every step can be explained later

items.definition: Recording any changes the investigator makes, because altered data may be inadmissible.
items.examples: Working only from a copy so the original is untouched.
items.examTip: Altered originals can be thrown out of court, so investigators use copies.
keyFacts: Record every action from seizure, so any change can be explained
Altered data may be inadmissible, because the court can't trust it
Work from copies, not the original, so the original evidence stays untouched

items.definition: Creating visual evidence and making sure findings are real, not false positives.
items.examTip: Too many false positives cause alert fatigue.
keyFacts: Photos, video and time-stamped screenshots show exactly what was found and when
Know your tools' error rates, so you can judge how far to trust their results
Manually review positives, so innocent files aren't wrongly flagged as evidence

items.term: Evidence of a Crime or Incident
items.definition: Deciding whether findings show a crime, a legal breach, a policy breach or another incident.
items.examples: Findings showing a hack, a GDPR breach or staff negligence.
items.examTip: Could be crime, a regulatory or contract breach, a policy breach, an attack or negligence.
keyFacts: Crime or regulatory breach, e.g. hacking under the Computer Misuse Act or a GDPR breach
Contract breach, e.g. a supplier failing to protect data as agreed
Internal policy breach, e.g. staff breaking the AUP, dealt with by disciplinary action
Attack, negligence or mismanagement, which decides who is responsible and what happens next

items.definition: Signs that a system has been compromised.
items.examples: Unusual traffic abroad; spikes in failed logins; odd DNS requests.
items.examTip: Indicators: unusual traffic, logins, DNS or port use, suspicious file changes.
keyFacts: Unusual traffic or destinations can mean data is being sent to an attacker
Unusual logins and DNS requests suggest stolen accounts or malware contacting its controller
Spikes in file reads and odd ports can mean data is being copied out
Suspicious file changes can mean malware has altered system files

items.definition: A structured report on the incident with recommendations to stop it happening again.
items.examples: A report analysing what went wrong and recommending policy and training changes.
items.examTip: Structure: title, contents, intro, headings, conclusions, citations.
keyFacts: Clear structure, so managers can quickly find what happened and what to do
Explain what went wrong and why detection was slow, so the same gaps aren't left open
Recommend improved policies, so procedures stop it happening again
Improve physical, software, hardware and training measures, so every weak area is addressed
